title: Ranita Leopardo
summary: An Angry Birds-inspired HTML5 game set in Corn Island: a catapult, destructible structures and a physics engine written from scratch, with no framework, no dependency and no external image.
role: Solo — the physics, the renderer, the levels, the audio synthesis and the PWA shell.
context: A game is a good excuse to write the parts a framework usually hides: collision detection, an impulse solver, a camera, particles and a deterministic loop. The setting is Corn Island, and everything on screen is drawn with vectors and Canvas.

solution.title: Custom 2D physics
solution.body: Bodies, broad-phase detection, AABB and SAT narrow-phase collision, manifolds resolved by clipping, and an impulse solver. Gravity, restitution and friction are the game's, not a library's.

solution.title: A deterministic loop
solution.body: `requestAnimationFrame` with a fixed 1/60 s physics timestep and an accumulator, so the simulation behaves the same on a 60 Hz phone and a 144 Hz monitor.

solution.title: Modular, dependency-free client
solution.body: Physics, rendering, camera, particles, lighting, scene, entities, UI and audio are separate modules under one namespace. Levels are JSON; the service worker makes the game installable and playable offline.

contribution: Solo project, built from scratch. The level design followed the mechanics: six hand-tuned levels that introduce the slingshot, the destructible materials and the enemy types in order.
approach: Writing the engine was the point, so the constraints were strict: no framework, no CDN, no external images, and it has to work by opening `index.html`. That rules out the usual shortcuts and forces the collision and render code to be small enough to debug by reading it. The trade-off is scope — this is a small game, not a general engine — and the code is organised so each subsystem can be understood alone.

technicalDecisions.title: SAT and clipping instead of pixel collision
technicalDecisions.body: Polygon-based collision produces a contact normal and a penetration depth, which is what an impulse solver needs to push bodies apart believably. Pixel tests would have been easier to start and impossible to make stable.

technicalDecisions.title: Fixed timestep
technicalDecisions.body: A variable timestep makes a slingshot shot depend on frame rate. The accumulator costs a little latency and buys reproducible levels, which is the difference between a puzzle and a lottery.

outcomes: The game runs from a static folder with no build step and no network dependency.
Six levels share one deterministic simulation, so a solution that works once works again.
Installing it to the home screen works offline, including the audio synthesised in the browser.
evidenceNote: Verified against the public rana-leopardo repository and its live deployment on 2026-11-25. No player count, retention or performance figure is published.
